lead: Engines and systems rarely fail without warning. Two minutes of checks each morning and an eye on the gauges prevent most breakdowns.

blocks.p: A diesel has no spark: it needs **fuel, air and compression**. Each morning check:

list: Oil, engine stopped, boat level. Milky oil means water in it: do not start.
Coolant in the header tank, engine cold.
The belt: about 1 cm of give under your thumb.
Raw-water seacock open, strainer clear, bilge dry, gear in neutral.

blocks.p: **Preheat** a cold engine for 10–15 seconds, start, and look for water at the exhaust at once. With the key at ON, the oil and charge lights and the buzzer are normal until she runs. Shift at idle, pausing in neutral. To stop, idle a few minutes first; never use the battery isolator.

lines: Key at ON, engine not yet started

sections.title: Water at the exhaust, or stop

blocks.p: Seawater carries the heat away: **seacock, strainer, impeller pump, heat exchanger**, then out with the exhaust. If little or none comes out, or the temperature alarm sounds, stop the engine and let it cool. Never open a hot coolant cap.

Look at the strainer first, then the impeller: find any broken vanes. A strong flow with the temperature still rising points to low coolant or a broken belt. If the engine will not fire, crank with the seacock closed, or water fills the exhaust and floods it; open it as soon as she runs.

head: Sign
Meaning
rows: Stop at once, check the oil

sections.title: Clean, free of air, and enough

blocks.p: Fuel runs from the tank through the **water separator**, the lift pump and the fine filter to the injectors. Water sinks to the bottom of the separator bowl: drain it. Dirty fuel makes the engine surge and stop: drain the separator, change the filter.
After running dry, or when a low tank lets the pickup suck air under heel, **bleed** the system: open the bleed screw and work the lift-pump lever until fuel runs without bubbles.

Range is usable fuel divided by hourly burn, times speed; the burn is litres refilled divided by engine hours. Easing the revs stretches it. At the fuel berth check the cap says DIESEL, switch off engine and electrics, and fill slowly with a rag at the breather.

sections.title: Prop walk and the pivot point

blocks.p: In astern the propeller kicks the stern sideways before the boat moves: **prop walk**, to port with a right-handed propeller. So berth port side-to, and turn short to starboard. With sternway on, the stern follows the wheel.

fig.note: Engine astern, rudder centred: stern walks to port

blocks.p: Going ahead she pivots a third of her length from the bow, and the stern swings wide. A catamaran spins on the spot: port engine ahead and starboard astern turn her to starboard.

fig.note: Turn to port: your stern swings to starboard

blocks.p: Vibration and lost speed mean a fouled propeller: stop, and clear it with the key out. Milky saildrive oil, or seawater on its diaphragm: report it. If the wheel goes slack, fit the emergency tiller; press Standby to take over from the autopilot.

A **starter battery** and a **house bank**: at anchor run everything from the house bank alone, and the engine will always start. A flat starter battery: parallel the banks, start, then separate them. Never open the isolator with the engine running: it destroys the alternator.

lines: Fridge and anchor light ran all night
Engine battery was isolated: she starts

blocks.p: Budget in **amp-hours**, amps times hours, and use only half of a lead-acid bank. Watts divided by 12 give the amps an inverter draws.

Replace a fuse like for like. A breaker or shore-power RCD that trips again at once is protecting you: find the fault. Connect the shore cable to the boat first, the pedestal last. Run the engine when you use the windlass; breaker off before hands go near the chain.

sections.title: Every hull fitting has a seacock

blocks.p: Fresh water: tank litres divided by the crew's daily use. A pump that runs on while the tap spits air has an empty tank; one that cuts in with every tap closed has a leak.

The **heads** take only what you have eaten and a little paper. In harbours and bays the Y-valve stays on the **holding tank**; empty it at a pump-out or well offshore, where rules allow. Close the heads seacocks at sea, or the bowl can siphon full when heeled.

A **seacock** is open with the handle along the pipe, closed across it. Leaking hose: close it. Broken fitting: hammer in the softwood bung. If the bilge pump keeps running, taste the water: fresh is a tank, salt is the sea.

Bottled gas is **heavier than air**, so its locker drains overboard and the drain must be clear. A solenoid valve at the bottle shuts the supply: after cooking switch it off first, let the flame die, then close the burner.
